Potential text:

Chapter One

By seven o'clock, the street on Mitali Chatterjee's map had moved two inches to the east, and no one else in the Survey room had noticed.

She stood before the drafting board with a ruler in one hand and a cold cup of tea in the other. The line for Pansura Lane—inked the evening before, still smelling of iron gall—now ran cleanly through a brickyard. In the place where it had been, the paper was blank, as if the lane had never been drawn at all.

"Miss Chatterjee?" Mr. Ashoke Sen, the field clerk, stood at the end of the table with the cautious expression he used when an error was about to be named. "Major Ferguson is asking why a municipal lane has entered a private property."

Mitali lifted the sheet by its corner. It was a great sheet, two feet wide, mounted on board and studded with brass tacks. The lane's new position was not smudged, not feathered, not the pale ghost of an erased line. It was crisp, black, and exactly the same thickness as the rest of the survey.

"It entered no private property," she said.

"The brickyard of Messrs. Ghose and Co. is on the 1884 plan."

"The 1884 plan is two years old. Brickyards are built. Lanes are opened. I measured Pansura Lane yesterday with a hundred-foot chain."

"You measured it here." He pointed to the blank strip of paper.

"I measured it where it was."

Ashoke glanced at the door, as if hoping Major Ferguson would intervene. The room was a long room above Chitter Avenue, with high windows, a ceiling fan that had lost one blade, and the permanent smell of India ink, damp paper, and the lime plaster that bloomed in the monsoon. Outside, Calcutta was waking: a cycle-rickshaw splashed through a puddle, a woman shouted the price of fish, and somewhere beyond Mirza Ghasem Street a temple bell struck six.

Mitali uncapped her pen and drew a fine line beside the moved street. It did not budge.

"Paper can shrink," Ashoke said.

"Paper shrinks everywhere," Mitali replied. "It does not shrink in one lane."

"Then perhaps the ink."

"The ink is dry."

She brought the map closer. The line had not merely shifted. Its relation to the surrounding streets was wrong. Pansura Lane should have begun at the northeast corner of the fish market and ended at the wall of a chowki. Now it began at the corner of a sweet-shop and ended at the boundary of a banyan tree that, on every map she had ever drawn, had not existed in that position.

Major Ferguson came then. He was a small Englishman with a large moustache and a habit of touching his spectacles as though they were his only remaining connection to reason. "I was told you have drawn a street into a brickyard," he said.

"I have drawn a street where I found it, Major."

"You found it yesterday."

"Yes."

"Yesterday there was a brickyard."

"There was a brickyard," Mitali said carefully. "And a lane. They were not in the same place."

He looked at the map. He looked at her. "A map does not wander, Miss Chatterjee."

"This one has."

Ashoke made a small sound that might have been laughter. Major Ferguson straightened. "You will correct the error."

"I will verify it."

"Will you?"

"With the chain."

He gave her a look that contained the entire history of his disappointment with Bengal, its monsoons, its servants, and, he clearly believed, its female draftsmen. "Do not bring me ghosts. Bring me measurements."

Mitali took the map down from the board. It was heavier than paper should be, all weight and rule. She rolled it with the care of a priest handling a sacred text, put it in her satchel, and took up the chain, the compass, and the field book.

The street outside was a red river of morning. A bullock cart groaned under a load of bricks; a boy in a white dhoti ran a skewer of kebabs through the steam of his stove; a woman balancing a brass pot of rice walked with the dignity of a general. Mitali moved through it with the flat of the map's corner under her arm and the chain coiled over her shoulder. The air was thick with coal smoke and the green rot of leaves. The monsoon had not yet begun, but the city already carried itself as if it were wet.

She reached the corner of Mirza Ghasem Street and the fish market at seven forty. The market was a long low shed of bamboo and tin, its floor stained brown with yesterday's blood. Fish lay on crushed snow in wooden boxes: hilsa, catla, mrigal, their silver skin flaking in the dust. A fishwife named Rani, whom Mitali had seen the previous day, was chopping a catla with a chopper so large it looked like a small door.

"Madam," Rani said, without looking up. "You are measuring us again?"

"I need to know where the lane begins."

"Where it has always begun." Rani nodded toward the corner of the sweet-shop, where a line of men waited for laddus. "You stood here yesterday with your little iron thing and made your marks. We thought you were counting our fish."

Mitali looked at the corner. The sweet-shop's shutter was half-raised. A sign in Bengali announced milk and laddus. Beyond it, Pansura Lane opened like a thin mouth: narrow, paved with broken brick, shaded by a banyan whose aerial roots hung like wet fingers. It ran east, as the map now showed it, into the dark mouth of the brickyard.

But the fish market was there too. It had not moved. The chowki wall was where it had always been. The lane had.

"This corner," Mitali said, "was not here yesterday."

Rani wiped her knife on her sari. "What corner?"

"The corner of the sweet-shop. The lane used to begin by the fish market."

Now the fishwife looked at her properly. "By the fish market? There is no lane by the fish market. There is a wall."

"There was a wall," Mitali said. "By the fish market. A brickyard wall."

Rani's face tightened. She glanced at the sweet-shop, then back. "You are not well, madam. Go home and drink tea. The heat is bad for the head."

But another voice came from the lane. A boy, no older than twelve, with a tin box of laddus on his hip, stood in the entrance. Mitali had seen him yesterday at the old corner, selling laddus beside the fish market. He had said, "Madam, if you measure the lane, do not measure it after the sun goes down. It is not quiet then."

"Here?" she asked.

The boy's eyes widened. "Yes, madam. Here."

"Yesterday you were by the fish market."

"I am by the sweet-shop."

"The sweet-shop was not here."

The boy swallowed a laddu from the rim of his box. "The sweet-shop has been here since my grandmother was a girl."

Mitali took out the field book. Her handwriting was small and slanted, the letters she had learned from her father. Under yesterday's date: Pansura Lane. Commencing N.E. angle fish market. Bearing N 10° E. 312 links. Terminus wall chowki. She had written it with such confidence that the page now felt like an accusation.

She uncoiled the chain. Ashoke had followed her, of course, because Ashoke followed her whenever the air suggested scandal. He stood under the banyan with his notebook open, looking as if he would rather be measuring a corpse.

"If you are going to measure," he said, "you might as well do it properly."

Mitali set the zero of the chain at the corner of the sweet-shop. "Stand here."

Ashoke stepped into the lane. It was so narrow that their shoulders nearly touched the walls. One wall was lime plaster, stained with turmeric and incense smoke. The other was brick, red and cracked, with a sign painted in white: GHOSE & CO. BRICKS. The lane smelled of fish, cow dung, and something sweet—jaggery, perhaps, or flowers left on a threshold.

"Stretch," Mitali said.

Ashoke stretched the chain with the bored precision of a man who had been doing it for ten years. "One hundred."

Mitali marked the ground with a little pinch of lime. "Again."

They moved forward, link by link. The lane was not straight. It bent slightly at the second hundred, where a drain ran down the middle, black and stinking. A woman sat outside a doorway washing a child's cloth. She watched them with an expression that was not hostility but recognition, as if she had seen them before and was waiting to see what would happen.

At the second hundred and fifty, the lane narrowed. The banyan's roots pressed down from above. In the darkness, Mitali heard the lane breathe: a faint dragging, like rope on stone, or like a long exhalation. She stopped.

"What is it?" Ashoke asked.

"Nothing."

"It sounded like something moving."

By seven o'clock, the street on Mitali Chatterjee's map had moved two inches to the east, and no one else in the Survey room had noticed.

She stood before the drafting board with a ruler in one hand and a cold cup of tea in the other. The line for Pansura Lane, inked the evening before and still smelling of lampblack, now ran cleanly through a brickyard. In the place where it had been, the paper was blank, as if the lane had never been drawn at all.

At this scale, two inches meant forty-three feet on the ground. Mitali had measured that lane with a hundred-foot chain. She had set the links at the northeast corner of the fish market, stretched them along the drain, marked the bend by the banyan, and noted the terminus at the chowki wall. The numbers were in her field book. The chain was in the store. Neither had learned to lie.

"Miss Chatterjee?" Ashoke Sen stood at the end of the table with the careful face he wore when an error was about to be named. "Major Ferguson is asking why a municipal lane has entered private property."

Mitali lifted the sheet by its corner. It was a great sheet, two feet wide, mounted on board and studded with brass tacks. The lane's new position was not smudged, not feathered, not the pale ghost of an erased line. It was crisp, black, and exactly the same thickness as the rest of the survey.

"It entered no private property," she said.

"The brickyard of Messrs. Ghose and Company is on the 1884 plan."

"The 1884 plan is seven years old. Brickyards are built. Lanes are opened. I measured Pansura Lane yesterday with a hundred-foot chain."

"You measured it here." He pointed to the blank strip of paper.

"I measured it where it was."

Ashoke glanced toward the door, as if hoping Major Ferguson would intervene. The room was a long room above Chitter Avenue, with high windows, a ceiling fan that had lost one blade, and the permanent smell of ink, damp paper, and lime plaster blooming in the October damp. Outside, Calcutta was waking: a cycle-rickshaw splashed through a puddle, a woman shouted the price of fish, and somewhere beyond Mirza Ghasem Street a temple bell struck six.

Major Ferguson came then. He was a small Englishman with a large moustache and a habit of touching his spectacles as though they were his only remaining connection to reason.

"I was told you have drawn a street into a brickyard," he said.

"I have drawn a street where I found it, Major."

"You found it yesterday."

"Yes."

"Yesterday there was a brickyard."

"There was a brickyard," Mitali said carefully. "And a lane. They were not in the same place."

He looked at the map. He looked at her. "A map does not wander, Miss Chatterjee."

"This one has."

Ashoke made a small sound that might have been laughter. Major Ferguson straightened. "You will correct the error."

"I will verify it."

"Will you?"

"With the chain."

He gave her a look that contained the entire history of his disappointment with Bengal, its monsoons, its servants, and, he clearly believed, its female draftsmen. "Do not bring me ghosts. Bring me measurements."

Mitali took the map down from the board. It was heavier than paper should be, all weight and rule. She rolled it with the care of a priest handling a sacred text, put it in her satchel, and took up the chain, the compass, and the field book.

The street outside was a red river of morning. A bullock cart groaned under a load of bricks; a boy in a white dhoti ran a skewer of kebabs through the steam of his stove; a woman balancing a brass pot of rice walked with the dignity of a general. Mitali moved through it with the flat of the map's corner under her arm and the chain coiled over her shoulder. The air was thick with coal smoke and the green rot of leaves. The city carried itself as if it were wet, though the sky was a hard white bowl.

She reached the corner of Mirza Ghasem Street and the fish market at seven forty. The market was a long low shed of bamboo and tin, its floor stained brown with yesterday's blood. Fish lay on crushed ice in wooden boxes: hilsa, catla, mrigal, their silver skin flaking in the dust. A fishwife named Rani, whom Mitali had seen the previous day, was chopping a catla with a chopper so large it looked like a small door.

"Madam," Rani said, without looking up. "You are measuring us again?"

"I need to know where the lane begins."

"Where it has always begun." Rani nodded toward the corner of the sweet-shop, where a line of men waited for laddus. "You stood here yesterday with your little iron thing and made your marks. We thought you were counting our fish."

Mitali looked at the corner. The sweet-shop's shutter was half-raised. A sign in Bengali announced milk and laddus. Beyond it, Pansura Lane opened like a thin mouth: narrow, paved with broken brick, shaded by a banyan whose aerial roots hung like wet fingers. It ran east, as the map now showed it, into the dark mouth of the brickyard.

But the fish market was there too. It had not moved. The chowki wall was where it had always been. The lane had.

"This corner," Mitali said, "was not here yesterday."

Rani wiped her knife on her sari. "What corner?"

"The corner of the sweet-shop. The lane used to begin by the fish market."

Now the fishwife looked at her properly. "By the fish market? There is no lane by the fish market. There is a wall."

"There was a wall," Mitali said. "By the fish market. A brickyard wall."

Rani's face tightened. She glanced at the sweet-shop, then back. "You are not well, madam. Go home and drink tea. The heat is bad for the head."

Another voice came from the lane. A boy, no older than twelve, with a tin box of laddus on his hip, stood in the entrance. Mitali had seen him yesterday at the old corner, selling laddus beside the fish market. He had said, in a voice too old for his face, "If you measure the lane, do not measure it after the sun goes down. It is not quiet then."

"Here?" she asked.

The boy's eyes widened. "Yes, madam. Here."

"Yesterday you were by the fish market."

"I am by the sweet-shop."

"The sweet-shop was not here."

"The sweet-shop has been here since my grandmother was a girl."

Ashoke stepped into the lane. It was so narrow that their shoulders nearly touched the walls. One wall was lime plaster, stained with turmeric and incense smoke. The other was brick, red and cracked, with a sign painted in white: GHOSE & CO. BRICKS. The lane smelled of fish, cow dung, and something sweet—jaggery, perhaps, or flowers left on a threshold.

"Stretch," Mitali said.

Ashoke stretched the chain with the bored precision of a man who had been doing it for ten years. "One hundred."

Mitali marked the ground with a little pinch of lime. "Again."

A woman sat outside a doorway washing a child's cloth. She watched them with an expression that was not hostility but recognition, as if she had seen them before and was waiting to see what would happen.

At the second hundred and fifty, the lane narrowed. The banyan's roots pressed down from above. In the darkness, Mitali heard the lane breathe: a faint dragging, like rope on stone, or like a long exhalation. She stopped.

"What is it?" Ashoke asked.

"Nothing."

"It sounded like something moving."

"It is a drain."

They completed the measurement. The lane was not 312 links. It was 318. Its bearing was not N 10° E but N 14° E. It ended not at the chowki wall but at a low door set into the brickyard wall, a door that had not been in the field book.

Mitali wrote the new numbers. The pencil moved as if it were tired.

Ashoke looked over her shoulder. "That is the same as the map."

"Yes."

"Then the map is correct."

"The map is not correct. The map is late."

He frowned. "What does that mean?"

Mitali did not answer. She was looking at the map in her hand. The line for Pansura Lane, which had been two inches east when she left the office, was now three inches east.

Ashoke saw her face. "Miss Chatterjee?"

The ink was dry.

She had not touched it.

The line had moved while she measured, while the sun climbed, while the city went about its morning. It had moved as if it were being drawn by someone on the other side of the paper.

"Show me," Ashoke whispered.

She held the sheet out. He leaned over. The line ran through the brickyard, through the banyan, through the low door at the lane's end, and on, across the map, into a stretch of ground marked only as empty.

"It is not moving," he said, though his voice had lost all authority.

"It is."

"Paper does not move."

"Paper," Mitali said, "does what it is told."

A shadow fell over them. The boy with the laddus stood in the entrance, his tin box empty. Behind him, the lane was empty too, though it had been full of people a moment before. The fishwife was gone. The woman with the washing cloth was gone. The low door at the end was open, and through it Mitali could see the brickyard: red bricks stacked to the sky, no lane at all.

"Where is it?" she asked.

The boy looked at the map. "It is where you have put it."

Mitali turned the sheet over. In the margin, where the scale was written, there was a new line of small print in her own handwriting:

Do not measure it after the sun goes down.

She had not written it.

She had.

She uncoiled the chain. Ashoke had followed her, because Ashoke followed her whenever the air suggested scandal. He stood under the banyan with his notebook open, looking as if he would rather be measuring a corpse.

"If you are going to measure," he said, "you might as well do it properly."

Mitali set the zero of the chain at the corner of the sweet-shop. "Stand here."

Ashoke stepped into the lane. It was so narrow that their shoulders nearly touched the walls. One wall was lime plaster, stained with turmeric and incense smoke. The other was brick, red and cracked, with a sign painted in white: GHOSE & CO. BRICKS. The lane smelled of fish, cow dung, and something sweet—jaggery, perhaps, or flowers left on a threshold.

"Stretch," Mitali said.

Ashoke stretched the chain with the bored precision of a man who had been doing it for ten years. "One hundred."

Mitali marked the ground with a little pinch of lime. "Again."

They moved forward, link by link. The lane was not straight. It bent slightly at the second hundred, where a drain ran down the middle, black and stinking. A woman sat outside a doorway washing a child's cloth. She watched them with an expression that was not hostility but recognition, as if she had seen them before and was waiting to see what would happen.

At the second hundred and fifty, the lane narrowed. The banyan's roots pressed down from above. In the darkness, Mitali heard the lane breathe: a faint dragging, like rope on stone, or like a long exhalation. She stopped.

"What is it?" Ashoke asked.

"Nothing."

"It sounded like something moving."

"It is a drain."

They completed the measurement. The lane was not 312 links. It was 318. Its bearing was not N 10° E but N 14° E. It ended not at the chowki wall but at a low door set into the brickyard wall, a door that had not been in the field book.

Mitali wrote the new numbers. The pencil moved as if it were tired.

Ashoke looked over her shoulder. "That is the same as the map."

"Yes."

"Then the map is correct."

"The map is not correct. The map is late."

He frowned. "What does that mean?"

Mitali did not answer. She was looking at the map in her hand. The line for Pansura Lane was exactly where the lane was. It had followed the lane, or the lane had followed it, and she could not say which.

Ashoke saw her face. "Miss Chatterjee?"

"The lane moved."

"Miss Chatterjee, lanes do not move."

"It did."

He looked at the map. He looked at the lane. He looked at the blank strip of air where the lane had been yesterday, and for a moment he did not speak at all.

They returned to the office before noon. Mitali put the map back on the board and tacked its corners with the patience of a woman who had learned that anger was a kind of error. Captain Ferguson studied it for a long time.

"If the lane has moved," he said at last, "then you will note the new position."

"Yes, sir."

"And if it moves again?"

Mitali met his eyes. "Then I will note that too."

He gave a thin smile that did not reach his spectacles. "You will not be responsible for the street. You will be responsible for the map."
